legacy_report: SOURCE: "Agentic-R1: Distilled Dual-Strategy Reasoning", Weihua Du, Pranjal Aggarwal, Sean Welleck, Yiming Yang (CMU LTI). arXiv 2507.05707v2, 30 Aug 2025. The header reads cs.CL; no venue is named in the text, so treat it as a preprint. COVERAGE: 54,555 of 54,555 chars read, all pages, appendices and references included. The extraction is clean. Table 1 cells are doubled (for example "37.059.3" means S=37.0, L=59.3). I parsed them by hand, and the Fig. 3 and Fig. 4 values are consistent with that reading. FIT TO TARGET NOTE: The paper does not address any of the four sections you named. It has no plan-writing with tools named, no state restatement, no DAG plans, and no choice among many tools. Its subject is one binary choice per problem, between Python code execution and text chain-of-thought, learned by distillation for math. The nearest fits are "choosing among tools" (the tool-or-no-tool decision) and the 10-call cap and executor loop. Do not cite it for the other three. CLAIMS (ranked) - Claim: The distilled 7B student beats both same-size baselines on the two tool-favouring benchmarks at the large budget. number: Agentic-R1-7B-SD scores 65.3 on DeepMath-L and 52.0 on Combinatorics300 at L, against 56.3 and 44.5 for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B. setup: Budgets S=4096 and L=32768 tokens, averaged over 5 seeds at T=0.6. DeepMath-L has 87 problems with answers above 10^5. Combinatorics300 has 300 problems. quote: "Agentic-R1-7B-SD (ours) SL 40.065.3 38.252.0 82.593.3 27.340.7 66.385.8 50.967.4" where: Table 1, p.5. - Claim: The average gain over the pure-reasoning baseline is large at the small budget and mostly gone before self-distillation at the large budget. number: At S the averages are 49.3 (Agentic-R1) and 50.9 (SD) against 47.4 for R1-Distill. At L they are 62.8 and 67.4 against 63.1. setup: Same as the previous claim. Reading the doubled cells: Agentic-R1 (pre-SD) averages 62.8 at L, which is below R1-Distill's 63.1. quote: "DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B SL 34.756.3 34.744.5 83.189.2 23.340.7 61.284.8 47.463.1" where: Table 1, p.5. - Claim: Tool use is chosen more often on tool-favouring problems, learned from supervised fine-tuning alone. number: At least one code call on 79.2% of Combinatorics300 problems, against 52.0% on AMC. setup: Agentic-R1, as the authors measured it. quote: "Agentic-R1 activates at least one code execution tool in 79.2% of the Combinatorics300 problems, while the usage of the tool drops to only 52.0% in the relatively simpler AMC dataset." where: p.5. - Claim: Composing trajectories (teacher A fails, teacher B corrects, with a transition sentence) beats training on single-teacher trajectories. number: At L, DeepMath-L 59.3% against 40.0%, AIME 40.7% against 34.0%, AMC 82.2% against 50.8%. setup: This is Table 2, the only ablation. It compares the pre-self-distillation student at the large budget. quote: "w/o composition 40.0% 34.0% 50.8% w/ composition 59.3% 40.7% 82.2%" where: Table 2, p.5. - Claim: A teacher weaker than the baseline can still lift the student above itself. number: The agentic teacher scores 48.4% on Combinatorics300. The student moves from 44.7% to 50.9%. setup: The teacher is OpenHands on Claude-3.5-Sonnet. The student's 50.9% is the SD model's score. Table 1 reports 52.0 for it at L, so the two figures disagree. quote: "the agentic strategy teacher achieves only 48.4% accuracy on Combinatorics300, yet after training, the student's performance improves significantly from 44.7% to 50.9%, surpassing the teacher." where: p.5. - Claim: The training set is small and the compute modest. number: 2,678 composed trajectories (685 both correct, 600 only first correct, 1393 first wrong then second correct). Fine-tuning took 12.7 hours on 4x A6000. setup: 4 epochs, AdamW, learning rate 1e-5. Self-distillation uses K=16 samples per problem, β1=0 and β2=0.9. quote: "the final distilled dataset contains 2, 678 examples"; "we use 4× A6000 GPUs for a total of 12.7 hours." where: App. A.2 and A.3.2, p.8. - Claim: Pure text reasoning is slow and the code loop is cheap by comparison. number: Up to 10 executor calls per problem, each capped at 3 s, so at most about 30 s extra. Text reasoning can take several minutes on 2xA6000. quote: "the language model is allowed to invoke a Python executor up to 10 times per problem, with each execution capped at 3 seconds." where: A.6, p.9. - Claim: The paper reports a regression on the simple benchmark. number: MATH500 at S is 80.0 (Agentic-R1) against 83.1 (R1-Distill). At L it is 82.4 against 89.2. quote: "we note a slight performance decrease in relatively simpler benchmarks (MATH500) compared to the pure text-reasoning model" where: p.4 and Table 1. BASELINES, compute-matched or not - The matching is by output tokens only. Accuracy at Budget truncates the trajectory at b tokens, with b equal to 4096 or 32768. Accuracy is `G(t_{0:min(b,L)}, a)`. - It is not matched on tool calls, wall-clock time, or executor tokens. Tool time is excluded from the budget. - Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (short-CoT) is flat across budgets (Fig. 3 shows about 0.329 to 0.331), so it never uses the larger budget. It is a weak foil. - Qwen w/ tool and w/o tool are different model families from the student. The student starts from R1-Distill, so the only same-base comparison is R1-Distill. - No baseline is another tool-integrated reasoning method such as ReTool, START or CoRT. Those are cited but not compared. - The grader gives R1-Distill a fairer deal: a fuzzy MathVerify match is used when the trace is truncated. LIMITS - Authors concede: - Transition phrases are hand-written, so output can read unnaturally. - The SD model may repeat itself. - 2.6k examples is probably too few to teach a new strategy from scratch. The base model already knew both modalities. - Not shown, my observation: - The Table 1 results are averages over 5 seeds with no variance or intervals reported. - The test sets are small (87 problems for DeepMath-L, and AIME 2025 has 30). - The benchmarks were chosen as tool-favouring (large answers), so the headline gains are on a hand-picked slice. - There is no ablation of self-distillation beyond Table 1, and none of the transition sentences. - Math only, with a single tool (Python). No evidence on planning, multi-tool selection, or non-math agents. - The 10-call cap and 3 s limit are fixed and were not varied. - The tool-choice decision is made by a fine-tuned model. This is not a prompt-time method, so it does not transfer to prompting-only settings. - Training uses first-teacher token budgets chosen at random (App. A.4.2). The second teacher is conditionally independent of y1: `π(·|x,y1)=π(·|x)`. This means the "correction" never actually sees the failed attempt. BUILDS ON: PaL (Gao et al., 2023) and PoT (Chen et al., 2023) for code-as-reasoning. ReAct (Yao et al., 2023), WebGPT (Nakano et al., 2022) and Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023) for interleaved tool calls. OpenHands (Wang et al., 2024) for the agentic teacher. DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025) and o1 (Jaech et al., 2024) for long-CoT. Cuadron et al. (2025) for the reasoning-action dilemma, the overthinking-with-tools failure the paper cites. ReTool (Feng et al., 2025), START and CoRT (Li et al., 2025a,b) and R1-Searcher / Search-R1 as the tool-plus-reasoning RL contrast. The distillation lineage is Sanh et al., 2019, Hsieh et al., 2023, and Li et al., 2024. Self-training: STaR (Zelikman et al., 2022) and Kumar et al., 2024. The budget curves draw on s1 (Muennighoff et al., 2025), L1 (Aggarwal and Welleck, 2025) and Wu et al., 2025. CODE - Algorithm 1 (DUALDISTILL, p.3) is the pseudocode. The composition rule is the part worth keeping: ```text case (0, 1): Add y1 ⊕ t−+ ⊕ y2 to T1 case (1, 1): Add y1 ⊕ t++ ⊕ y2 to T1 case (1, 0): Add y1 to T1 ``` - Transition sentences (Table 4, p.9): "Wait, the code is not correct, let's try text reasoning." / "Wait, use text reasoning is too tedious, let's try code reasoning." / "Wait, we can also use {B}-reasoning as an alternative way to verify the solution." - Inference prompt (Fig. 2, p.9): the system prompt asks for ``, `` and `` tags. An executor runs the code and returns output inside ``. - Loop (A.6): generation pauses on the `` token, the code runs, and the feedback is appended in `` tags before inference resumes. FIGURES - Fig. 1, p.1: the DualDistill overview with two teachers, composition, and self-distillation. It explains the method faster than the prose. - Fig. 3, p.10: average accuracy against token budget from 1448 to 32768. It shows the Agentic-R1 advantage at small budgets and the flat Qwen lines. It is the best candidate for a figure in your note, as it makes the "choose between text and tool" trade-off visible at a glance. - Fig. 4, p.10: the same curves per benchmark. - Figs. 5 to 7, pp.11, 14, 15: full trajectories. Fig. 6 shows tool to text after failed code. Fig. 7 shows text to a DP code solution, with a second check. - I did not run the captions script, since the captions above came from the extraction. PROBLEMS - No embedded instructions found in the PDF text. - Table 1 cells are doubled and need parsing. The 50.9 against 52.0 mismatch for Combinatorics300 (prose against Table 1) is unexplained. The prose figure of 50.9 matches the S column of the SD model, which suggests the text compares a small-budget student score to a teacher score of unstated budget. - The paper is math-only and does not support claims about planning, DAGs, state restatement or many-tool selection. Citing it for those would be a mistake.
